title: Permutation Groups and the Symmetric Group
quickIdea: The bijections of a set form a group under composition, the symmetric group S_n of order n!, and it is the standard source of non-abelian examples.
remember: For a set A the bijections from A to itself form a group under composition: the composition of bijections is a bijection, the identity map is the identity, and the inverse map is the inverse. GATE CSE 1996 Q.2.4 uses this as one of its true options.
For A = {1, ..., n} this is the symmetric group S_n and |S_n| = n!: 2, 6, 24 and 120 for n = 2, 3, 4, 5.
S_1 and S_2 are abelian; S_n is non-abelian for every n >= 3, since (1 2)(1 2 3) = (2 3) while (1 2 3)(1 2) = (1 3).
Permutations are written in cycle notation, disjoint cycles commute, and a cycle of length k has order k.
The order of a permutation is the lcm of its disjoint cycle lengths, so (1 2)(3 4 5) has order 6.
S_3 has six elements: the identity, three transpositions of order 2 and two 3-cycles of order 3; its subgroup orders are 1, 2, 3 and 6, all divisors of 6.
The even permutations form the alternating group A_n of order n!/2, the kernel of the sign homomorphism.

example.prompt: In S_3 compute (1 2)(1 2 3) and (1 2 3)(1 2), reading right to left.
example.work: (1 2)(1 2 3): 1 goes to 2 then to 1, 2 goes to 3 and stays at 3, 3 goes to 1 then to 2, giving (2 3). (1 2 3)(1 2): 1 goes to 2 then to 3, 2 goes to 1 and stays at 1, 3 goes to 3 then to 2, giving (1 3).
example.answer: The two products are (2 3) and (1 3), which differ, so composition in S_3 is not commutative.

gateAngle: Reach for S_3 whenever a question needs a small non-abelian group: it has order 6, so it is the smallest one, and it is the standard counterexample to 'small order means abelian' beyond order 5.

variations.label: CONCEPTUAL PRACTICE QUESTION
variations.question: What is the order of the permutation (1 2 3 4)(5 6) in S_6?
variations.answer: 4, the lcm of the cycle lengths 4 and 2.
variations.why: The order is the lcm of the disjoint cycle lengths, never their sum or their product.

variations.label: ORIGINAL PYQ-STYLE QUESTION
variations.question: How many elements of S_4 have order 2?
variations.answer: Nine: the six transpositions plus the three double transpositions such as (1 2)(3 4).
variations.why: Order 2 means a product of disjoint transpositions, so the count is by cycle shape, not by trying elements one at a time.

variations.label: PREDICTED VARIATION
variations.question: Do the permutations of {1, ..., n} that fix the element 1 form a subgroup?
variations.answer: Yes: they are exactly the permutations of the remaining n - 1 elements, so they form a copy of S_(n-1) inside S_n, of order (n - 1)!.
variations.why: The set of permutations fixing a point is the stabiliser of that point, the smallest instance of a group acting on a set.

trap.what: Assuming composition commutes because it looks like multiplication, and assuming |S_n| = n.
trap.why: The group of permutations of n objects has n! elements, and it is non-abelian from n = 3, so the order of the two factors in a product matters.

check.question: How many elements does S_4 have, and is it abelian?
check.answer: 24 = 4!, and it is not abelian, because the two products of (1 2) and (1 2 3) differ.
check.explanation: The bijections of a 4-element set are 4! = 24, and the pair of permutations above gives a counterexample to commutativity. In general S_n is non-abelian for every n >= 3, and S_3 already shows it.
